FWIW I think we could do the following:

  1. use the Lean4Lean spec without inductives. (Yes, inductives are the missing piece, but instead you can use lean-inductive-models to convert a proof with inductives to one without.) (And yes, this spec is about to change but no reason to not let someone verify their kernel now.)
  2. give a full proof that this fragment is consistent (relative to ZFC with countably many inaccessible cardinals). There is a branch of lean4lean-model where this is almost done.
  3. one can prove their kernel is sound (not complete) relative to the spec. (If it’s a lean kernel they can prove functional correctness in Lean, assuming they trust the lean compiler. If it’s a rust kernel, they can prove a shallow embedding is functionally correct, assuming they trust the shallow embedding. If it’s a WASM kernel, they can prove the byte code is correct up to a deep embedding.)
  4. Run this kernel with lean-inductive-models translation.

Another (slightly different) approach to tackling this problem is modelling the Lean kernel in something like mm0 which has seen some experimentation, also by Mario Carneiro. Instead of writing an executable kernel that gets verified, you write an executable kernel that relays the steps taken by the kernel to an even simpler verifier which only needs to check the validity of the steps taken by the kernel (where there's some soundness guarantee about this simpler verifier). While this is doable in something like HOL light as well, I don't know how well other systems would handle the very large proofs/traces that would be involved.

On paper this approach has some attractive properties in that (1) it doesn't rely on Lean, (2) the foundational system used by the verifier can be much simpler than Lean's foundations, and (3) the verifier itself can be written to have more attractive safety properties when it doesn't have also be a proof assistant for research mathematics, but I think mm0 as an ecosystem is a much longer time horizon project. I'm unsure whether there are downsides other than the work required to actually implement and prove properties about the tools that may have motivated the prioritization of lean4lean.

@Chris Bailey As for converting Lean to MetaMath, I think there are two possibilities:

  1. Convert from Lean to MetaMath or MM0 using the same logic/type theory rules as Lean (Metamath/Lean). While @Mario Carneiro has a toy version of this, I think the actual type theory of Lean has changed (and this is one thing creating a lot of confusion around verifying Lean since we don't yet know what Lean even is formally or if the full type theory is consistent, right?).
  2. Converting to a ZFC-like set theory, like MetaMath/set.mm but with a few more axioms. I think @Elliot Glazer has worked out the details. I still get a bit confused myself if the final set theory can be ZFC + omega many inaccessibles or if it has to be the more exotic ZFC+PFIRS. (I think it depends on the Lean statement being converted and if we want the conversion to be a bijection of statements between Lean and the set theory or just one-directional. See here and here.) But to do this, again, we need to know Lean's actual type theory is consistent, since this is basically building an explicit set-theoretic interpretation of Lean.

So until we have a formal spec of Lean, I don't know how we will convert to MetaMath using either approach. (But I guess we can just pick some spec, including the lean-inductive-models interpretation, which is known to be consistent by Mario's thesis [but maybe not complete].)

But both Lean-to-MM approaches require handling kernel reduction, which MetaMath and mm0 don't support. See this PA.SX question about this with three possibilities:

  1. Trace the full kernel reduction and run every single reduction step in MetaMath.
  2. Use MM0 tactics to do the reduction on the fly (similar to the LCF approach).
  3. Add reduction as a native feature of the MM0 checker (similar to the dependent type theory approach).

I can now think of a fourth option:

  1. Use AI to convert long kernel reductions to compact explicit steps to prevent long traces. This is sort of imitating what humans do in MathMath/set.mm.

@Jason Rute Converting lean to MM0 is ultra tedious. I've checked the lean formal spec in mm0 and it's missing Quotient.ind or something. So I didn't bother that much. But in general you would have to get rid of all kernel extensions, natLit, defeq and you would need to specify each step that those derivations do. mm0 has also some non-repeatablity expressions that are build into it. So during the export you would need to make sure that the stack is set up correctly and that every duplicated subexpression is referenced from the stack.

But I think the biggest challenge is just getting natLits to play nice. I've thought about defining hex values 0x00 to 0xff and converting natLits to them. Then you would have 256⋅256256\cdot 256256⋅256 theorems for just addition and multiplication, so that you can do bytewise addition and multiplication.

Another problem will be heavy defeqs. A subexpression in the lean kernel language may only be few bytes, but this expanded to a mm0 proof could be unbounded as typechecking is undecidable. I'm really curious how expensive in terms of bytes some of the heaviest defeqs in mathlib are.

But both Lean-to-MM approaches require handling kernel reduction, which MetaMath and mm0 don't support. See this PA.SX question about this with three possibilities:

  2. Use MM0 tactics to do the reduction on the fly (similar to the LCF approach).
  3. Add reduction as a native feature of the MM0 checker (similar to the dependent type theory approach).

I can now think of a fourth option:

  1. Use AI to convert long kernel reductions to compact explicit steps to prevent long traces. This is sort of imitating what humans do in MathMath/set.mm.

One of the other options floated at the time (and which I liked) was to do just beta reduction natively in mm0, and then use (1) the rest of the time. Beta reduction would be a pretty significant portion of the trace volume while also being something one could pretty confidently implement natively. At the time of these discussions the main bottleneck was developer cycles, it may very well be the case that 2 would be much more tractable now.

Yes, that's the idea. This would be Jason's first list item: "Trace the full kernel reduction and run every single reduction step in MetaMath." The verifier can rely on a much smaller TCB and be simpler in its construction. It can be built on simpler foundations as well, which may or may not be of interest to any particular user.

Setting aside the "native beta reduction" thing mentioned above, the proof traces you're going to get with this approach will be enormous. Not like "impossible with today's computers" enormous, but they would likely have to be streamed from the producer to the verifier and would need a verifier written with performance in mind.

@Chris Bailey I don't think the point is about how difficult beta reduction is to implement. The biggest benefit of mm0 and metamath is that it's a really simple system.

I would suggest an absolute minimal prelude with a debloated Lean.Expr equivalent. In particular the prelude can only contain lean's typing rules (all explicit), all three standard axioms and the definitions that are needed to state them. In particular Iff, Eq for propext, Eq for Quot.sound and Nonempty for Classical.choice. Nothing else, not even Nat should be part of the prelude.

For Lean.exprs just bvar, sort, const, app, lam and forallE. All other could in principle be removed I think. Anything that uses natLit is converted into a "suitable" representation (just like metamath does it), proj can be written in terms of recursors, letE can likely be put on the stack, mdata is not needed, same with mvar and fvar can be converted to bvar.

The benefits of having the lowest possible representation is that you can do crazy cool stuff that you otherwise couldn't do, certain optimisations are possible because you can tell the verifier the exact steps you want to do to eke out performance.

Remember that you don't remove it from the language, you just put it a layer or more above it.

The reason I'd like that theorem---or better yet, the theorem which also has second-order quantifiers over functions Nat -> Nat or higher-order quantifiers over functions (Nat -> Nat) -> Nat, ((Nat -> Nat) -> Nat) -> Nat and so on---is that a large amount of mathematics can be encoded in this form, including the Riemann Hypothesis, Navier-Stokes, P vs NP, all as first-order arithmetic formulas. Even more mathematics is encodable in second- or third-order arithmetic.

This would show three things: (1) It would ensure the logical consistency strength isn't especially high. For example, I recently saw a comment (maybe mistaken) that made me think some interpretation of mutual inductives in one external checker could prove the existence of a Mahlo cardinal. Mathematicians wouldn't like a proof of NS using Mahlo cardinals. :smile: (2) It would show theorems which contract ZFC aren't provable in Lean, like "all reals are computable" (which is a second-order statement). (3) And it would guard against being able to prove extra theorems that are not true in standard "ZFC + large cardinals" theories. I can't think of natural examples arising from real type theories (and maybe there are none), but the Rosser sentence ("For any proof of me, there is a shorter proof of my negation") is a fun first-order example, and the continuum hypothesis is a third-order example. Neither contradicts Lean nor increases the consistency strength.

Since ordinary second-order ZFC is equiconsistent with ZFC + 1 inaccessible, I would expect the theory described in con-leche to be equiconsistent with ZFC + "there exists omega many inaccessibles with an inaccessible above them". Since the statement in the README says that a model of its set theory can be constructed using lean4lean-model's version of ZFC + "there exists omega many inaccessibles", I was intrigued.

The definition in lean4lean-model is this:

/--
There are `ω` inaccessible cardinals: a strictly increasing `ℕ`-indexed sequence of them, one to
interpret each Lean universe `Sort 0, Sort 1, ...`.

Lean itself cannot prove this: its foundations give only `v`-many inaccessibles in universe `v`
(`Cardinal.IsInaccessible.univ`), i.e. a numeral's worth for any fixed universe, never `ω` of
them in a single `Cardinal.{u}`. That gap is exactly the consistency strength the theorem below
assumes, and is why this is a hypothesis rather than a lemma.
-/
def OmegaInaccessibles : Prop :=
  ∃ κ : ℕ → Cardinal.{u}, StrictMono κ ∧ ∀ n, (κ n).IsInaccessible

The description in the comment does not match the definition. The definition asserts omega many inaccessibles in every universe simultaneously. If I am not mistaken, Lean with this axiom should have the consistency strength of ZFC + "there exist omega + omega many inaccessibles".
this is actually a family of definitions, one for each universe, the version for universe u saying "there are omega many inaccessibles strictly less than Cardinal.univ.{u}"
there is no way to take as a hypothesis a statement of the form "XXX holds for all universes"

I find this equivalent statement to be clearer with its relation to ordinals:

import Mathlib.SetTheory.Cardinal.Regular
axiom omega :
    ∃ κ : {o : Ordinal.{v} // o < Ordinal.omega0} ↪o Cardinal.{u},
      ∀ o, (κ o).IsInaccessible

if you add a universe polymorphic axiom with that type you do probably get bumped up to ZFC + {"there are omega + n many inaccessibles" | n a numeral}
in fact the axiom for a lower universe always implies the version for any higher universe, so you get the same effect just assuming OmegaInaccessibles.{0}

This is not really true. Second-order ZFC usually does not guarantee that you can use your top-level inaccessible $I$, and do various set-theoretical bussiness with it (computing e.g. ℵI+\aleph_{I^+}ℵI+​). So I find it more accurate to say "set theory + omega inaccessibles" than "set theory + omega inaccessibles + 1".

I find the con-leche approach quite reasonable, and I am not a big fan of first-order (axiom schemas are weird). For me, a downside of this is that it is strictly stronger than Lean.

If one wanted, it would be possible to do ensure consistency of this within Lean through limiting the number of universes in compile time. Then the set-theory would take a parameter n as the bound on the universes, and the inaccessibles chain would be just univChain : Fin n → V. In Lean, it could be then possible to construct something like

def SetTheory.raise.{u} {V : Type u} (n : Nat) (st : SetTheory.{u} V n) :
    Σ V2 : Type (u+1), SetTheory.{u+1} V2 (n+1) := sorry

Have you considered that? The checker itself would then have to count the universes, and possibly error out on "universe overflow, please compile with more universes" :grinning: .

Yes, this has been discussed a few times. The induction is then left as an exercise to the reader :-)

I think the best thing would be to rely on MathLib's existing formalization of the semantics of first-order logic, with ZFC + inaccessibles stated as usual in the language of a single relation symbol (and maybe countably many constants for inaccessibles if it would make things easier). The obvious analogue of what con-leche has done thusfar would be to assume that a model exists of this theory.

The Completeness Theorem of FOL has not been upstreamed into Mathlib yet, but if it were, then a better version would be to assume that your set theory is merely consistent and then apply the Completeness Theorem to get a model.

It could be that con-leche is using second-order Replacement in some nontrivial way that can't easily be eliminated (and maybe I should try to search through the proof to look for evidence of this), but from past informal work on set-theoretic semantics of type theory I don't understand why this would be necessary.

Second-order ZFC usually does not guarantee that you can use your top-level inaccessible $I$, and do various set-theoretical bussiness with it (computing e.g. ℵI+\aleph_{I^+}ℵI+​). So I find it more accurate to say "set theory + omega inaccessibles" than "set theory + omega inaccessibles + 1".

I was speaking in terms of consistency strength relative to ordinary first-order ZFC. My statement is a standard consequence of Zermelo's quasi-categoricity theorem for second-order ZF(C), but this is of course itself a theorem of ZF(C) whose statement does not have an unambiguous translation to Lean, so perhaps the situation is different for second-order ZF(C) formalized in Lean. This sort of uncertainty is one of the reasons why first-order foundations gained such popularity.

I find the con-leche approach quite reasonable, and I am not a big fan of first-order (axiom schemas are weird). For me, a downside of this is that it is strictly stronger than Lean.

For a project like con-leche, it doesn't really matter what any individual thinks. For the wider mathematical community, ZF(C) definitely means first-order ZF(C), so con-leche's README is arguably a bit misleading at the moment by failing to mention this caveat. Given the current social currents around both Lean's foundations and the usage of AI to autonomously produce large proof developments, a project that is using AI to autonomously produce theorems/proofs about Lean's foundations should probably be as clear as possible on the outer shell that is exposed to human readers.

I think the best thing would be to rely on MathLib's existing formalization of the semantics of first-order logic, with ZFC + inaccessibles stated as usual in the language of a single relation symbol (and maybe countably many constants for inaccessibles if it would make things easier).

You probably also want to add a symbol for a choice function so that you can express the Axiom of Global Choice. ZF + Global Choice in this extended language is conservative over ZFC, but that's probably not a result whose proof you want to include in the scope of the project.
